findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Capture the child-environment projection model and the per-adapter secret-name registry contract in an ADR / AGENTS.md / design-doc update so the isolation invariants are durable.
evidence: 'Add src/rebar/_child_env.py with a pure environment projection API and a checked-in registry of exact secret names owned by each Rebar adapter.'
No ADR / AGENTS.md / design-doc capture is named for this new pattern/registry contract.
findings.finding: The plan introduces a novel cross-cutting architectural pattern — a shared child-environment projection API (`_child_env.py`) plus a checked-in registry of exact secret names owned per Rebar adapter — but does not capture this decision in an ADR / AGENTS.md / design-doc update. The projection rules (trusted same-capability inherit ambient, owning children get overlay, siblings strip exact declared names, native chains stay ambient, never mutate os.environ) are load-bearing invariants future maintainers must not violate.
scenarios: A future adapter author adds a secret but forgets to register its name, so unrelated siblings leak it — with no documented invariant explaining the registry's purpose.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a plan step to record an ADR (or AGENTS.md section) documenting the projection rules and the adapter-owned secret-name registry as the authoritative contract new adapters must extend.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the positive rationale for the name-denylist child-env projection (why strip-declared-names-and-inherit-the-rest is chosen over a default-deny allowlist), naming the native-SDK/helper-chain compatibility constraint that makes an allowlist infeasible and acknowledging the leak-on-unregistered-name residual risk.
evidence: Outcome: 'unrelated siblings remove exact secret names declared by other Rebar adapters, unknown native Git/SSH/AWS/proxy/CA variables survive'
Plan step 2: 'a checked-in registry of exact secret names owned by each Rebar adapter. The registry contains names, never values; native SDK/helper chains remain ambient.'

The plan asserts WHAT survives but not WHY a name-denylist is chosen over a default-deny allowlist; the WHY (native SDK/helper chains break under an allowlist) is implied by a requirement but never given as a rationale for the design choice.
findings.finding: The plan specifies the child-env projection as a denylist (strip only the exact declared secret NAMES; let all unknown native Git/SSH/AWS/proxy/CA variables survive) but never states the POSITIVE rationale for choosing a denylist over a more restrictive default-deny allowlist — which is the load-bearing security trade-off for this security-tagged story.
scenarios: A future adapter adds a new secret name and forgets to register it; under a denylist it leaks to unrelated siblings, whereas an allowlist would have failed closed — the reader cannot tell from the plan whether this residual risk was consciously accepted.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a one-line rationale to Plan step 2 / Outcome, e.g. 'A name-denylist (not a default-deny allowlist) is chosen because native Git/SSH/AWS/proxy/CA and SDK helper chains rely on arbitrary ambient variables an allowlist cannot enumerate; the residual risk (an unregistered secret name leaks) is bounded by the checked-in registry being the single audited enumeration of adapter send-credential names.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Justify the denylist secret-name projection against an allowlist alternative (or document/mitigate the fail-open exposure when a secret name is absent from the adapter registry).
evidence: Outcome: 'unrelated siblings remove exact secret names declared by other Rebar adapters, unknown native Git/SSH/AWS/proxy/CA variables survive'
Step 2: 'a checked-in registry of exact secret names owned by each Rebar adapter'

Prior art (credential-broker CLIs, 12-factor, subprocess env scrubbing) generally favors allowlisting known-safe names over denylisting known-bad names for a security boundary, because a denylist fails open for any name not enumerated
Repo confirms the denylist model is the intended design: _child_env.py registry is 'NAMES, never VALUES' and 'unrelated' removes adapter-owned names while unknown vars survive
findings.finding: The plan isolates unrelated-sibling child environments with a denylist (strip exact secret names declared in the Rebar adapter registry; let all unknown variables survive) but does not weigh this against the established secure-by-default alternative of an allowlist, so a secret whose name is not yet in the registry (new/renamed adapter var, or a third-party secret) silently leaks to unrelated siblings.
findings.location: Plan Outcome / step 2; AC 'unrelated siblings omit every other adapter's exact declared secret name'
scenarios: A new Rebar adapter or a renamed secret env-var whose name has not yet been added to the registry is inherited by an unrelated sibling child
A third-party or operator-set secret that is not a Rebar-declared name survives projection into an unrelated sibling
